transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-22
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Ava Martinez, Liam O'Connor (Redwood); Priya Desai, Marcus Lee, Sophie Brown (Nimbus Health)

Summary:
- Quick review of last week's runs, updated results on continous batching and concurrency tuning, decisions on soak tests and next benchmarks.

--- Transcript body ---
00:00 Speaker 1 (Ava): hey everyone thanks for joining, quick check on timing we've got 45 minutes, main goals: see the latest throughput numbers and agree soak/next steps, Liam do you want to kick off with results?
00:17 Speaker 2 (Liam): yeah sure, thanks ava. so last week we pushed the continuous batching change and increased target concurrency from 16 to 32. quick summary: steady-state tok/s improved by ~1.9x vs baseline, CPU/GPU util looked good, but we saw p99 tail creep by about 120-150ms on longer sequences.
00:45 Speaker 3 (Priya): when you say continuous batching, is that the change to the dynamic batch window and queue depth? we tuned the window to 30ms and queue depth to 128, right?
00:58 Speaker 2 (Liam): correct, dynamic window at 30ms with a soft cap on batch size 64 and queue depth 128. importantly we enabled prefix caching for common prompts so KV cache hits were around 22% which helped reduce per-token work on repeated sessions.
01:20 Speaker 4 (Marcus): i noticed in the logs there were a few spikes where q depth jumped to 180, was that overflow or some burst pattern?
01:28 Speaker 2 (Liam): that was an artifact of the client-side retry combined with a short network blip; the server queue accepted them but the batching window elongated which pushed some requests into the next batch and increased tail. we put a smoothing lambda on ingress in today's run to drop duplicates and that reduced spikes.
01:47 Speaker 3 (Priya): ok. what about concurrency targets beyond 32? did you try 64?
01:52 Speaker 2 (Liam): we did a limited run at 64 for 15 minutes; got further throughput gains but p99 jumped more noticeably, and GPU memory pressure increased due to more KV state and longer live tensors. so 64 is viable with more memory and a slightly more aggressive quantized model — or we can use model sharding. but for the POC scope, 32 looks like the sweet spot for cost/latency.
02:15 Speaker 1 (Ava): sophie, does that align with your SLA expectations?
02:20 Speaker 5 (Sophie): yeah we have a 200ms p95 SLA for interactive features; p99 we want below 400ms ideally. the current 32-run had p95 at ~160ms and p99 ~420ms, so p99 is slightly above target. we can accept a small deviation during pilot if the average costs drop materially.
02:40 Speaker 3 (Priya): what's 'materially'? are we talking 15% cost reduction? 30%?
02:47 Speaker 1 (Ava): from Redwood's bench it was about 18-22% unit cost reduction moving from 16->32 with continuous batching + KV cache. i'll send a short calc after the call.
03:00 Speaker 4 (Marcus): any concern about warm-up or cold start tail? we noticed initial p99s were worse for new instances.
03:07 Speaker 2 (Liam): yes, warm-up affects the early window. we recommend a small pre-warm traffic ramp (10-15 minutes) or using reserved instances (Dedicated) for production to avoid that. For the POC we can add a warm-up phase to the soak test.
03:27 Speaker 3 (Priya): on the queueing side, what are recommended thresholds? current setup 128 queue depth soft, 64 hard?
03:33 Speaker 2 (Liam): our recommended config: soft queue depth = 128, hard cap = 192. Helm the ingress to enforce client-side rate-limiting to avoid bursts; also set max-batches-in-flight to 8 so we limit parallelism and reduce GPU context switching.
03:50 Speaker 5 (Sophie): is there a tradeoff between max-batches-in-flight and overall throughput?
03:54 Speaker 2 (Liam): yes, fewer batches-in-flight reduces tail but can reduce peak throughput. it's a tuning knob: for interactive UX we bias lower (4-8), for background batching we bias higher.
04:08 Speaker 3 (Priya): security/compliance check — any changes here that affect logs or data residency? we need to ensure KV cache doesn't leak PHI to logs.
04:17 Speaker 1 (Ava): good point — KV cache is in-memory only and we don't persist cache to disk; logs redact prompt text by default in the POC unless you enable debug mode. we also support KMS for customer-managed keys in private deployment; i'll attach the security note after the call.
04:36 Speaker 6 (Sophie?): (overlap) can we get SOC2 details?
04:39 Speaker 1 (Ava): yes, we have SOC 2 Type II report and ISO artifacts; i'll share the security packet.
04:46 Speaker 2 (Liam): back to perf: we also measured latency vs sequence length. short sequences (<=64 tokens) benefited most from batching; long sequences saw smaller improvement because attention compute dominates and batching adds queuing. so recommend lowering batching window for long seq workloads.
05:10 Speaker 3 (Priya): did you try adaptive windowing? like smaller window for long seq sessions?
05:14 Speaker 2 (Liam): we tried a naive approach — per-client hint to set window to 10ms for long sequences. results mixed. Better approach is dynamic windowing that uses expected sequence length distribution; we can prototype that next week.
05:32 Speaker 4 (Marcus): what about model quantization? any impact with continuous batching?
05:36 Speaker 2 (Liam): quantization reduces memory footprint and allows higher concurrency but can slightly change output quality. for throughput testing we used q4_0 for the mid-tier model; we can run a quality regression on sample prompts.
05:50 Speaker 1 (Ava): ok let's walk through the numbers quickly — liam you had a slide right?
05:54 Speaker 2 (Liam): (narrates) baseline: concurrency 16, continuous batch off -> 1200 tok/s, p95 170ms, p99 360ms. With continuous batching + concurrency 32 -> 2300 tok/s, p95 160ms, p99 420ms. 64-run peaked 3400 tok/s but p99 rose to ~650ms.
06:18 Speaker 3 (Priya): those numbers are clearer, thanks. are these per-GPU or cluster-wide?
06:23 Speaker 2 (Liam): per-GPU across the dedicated test pool, cluster numbers scale linearly but you need to account for network egress and broker saturation.
06:32 Speaker 5 (Sophie): for our budget we can't afford big dedicated capacity yet — prefer hosted but want predictable latency. any recommendations?
06:40 Speaker 1 (Ava): for predictable latency, Redwood Dedicated is best; for cost-saving during pilot, hosted with reserved warm-up and the tuning we discussed is fine. we can propose a hybrid: hosted with reserved capacity for peak hours.
06:58 Speaker 4 (Marcus): will the KV cache be per-tenant or per-process? curious about memory isolation.
07:03 Speaker 2 (Liam): per-tenant within the process, isolated namespaces. memory accounting is per-tenant and we can set cache size limits per customer.
07:15 Speaker 3 (Priya): ok good. question: when you say queue depth 128, does that add extra latency for single-shot requests if traffic is low?
07:23 Speaker 2 (Liam): no — if traffic is low batch will form quickly and window will close early. queue depth only matters under load or bursts.
07:33 Speaker 1 (Ava): quick poll — are we comfortable calling concurrency=32 the pilot target?
07:38 Speaker 5 (Sophie): yes, tentative yes.
07:40 Speaker 3 (Priya): yes, pending soak results.
07:42 Speaker 4 (Marcus): yes.
07:44 Speaker 1 (Ava): great. next we agreed soak test details?
07:47 Speaker 2 (Liam): proposed soak: 1 hour at concurrency=32 with a 15-minute warm-up ramp, synthetic distribution matching production seq length, collect p50/p95/p99, GPU util, kv hit rate, and traces. Priya will run this.
08:05 Speaker 3 (Priya): i'll run it tomorrow and upload logs to the shared folder, link?
08:09 Speaker 1 (Ava): i'll drop link in the thread.
08:11 Speaker 2 (Liam): also i'll push the updated config (window 30ms, soft queue 128, hard 192, max-batches-in-flight 8) to the repo and include notes on the smoothing lambda we used.
08:24 Speaker 3 (Priya): about retries, any recommended client retry backoff to avoid bursts?
08:28 Speaker 2 (Liam): exponential backoff with jitter, initial backoff 50ms and cap 500ms. avoid synchronous retry for user-facing requests.
08:38 Speaker 5 (Sophie): can you clarify cost implications if we go to steady concurrency 32 vs 16?
08:43 Speaker 1 (Ava): i'll send a calc — roughly 18-22% lower unit-cost with 32 due to better GPU utilization, but peak spend may be higher during bursts. we'll model for your traffic pattern.
08:56 Speaker 4 (Marcus): any legal/procurement blockers if we move from hosted to dedicated later?
09:01 Speaker 1 (Ava): procurement-wise we can start hosted, then convert credits to a committed dedicated contract; legal will take standard 4-6 weeks for enterprise terms. For private on-prem there's longer lead time.
09:12 Speaker 3 (Priya): ok timeline: run soak tomorrow, share logs same day, we reconvene next Thursday for review — that works for us.
09:20 Speaker 1 (Ava): perfect. quick recap of action items...
09:24 Speaker 2 (Liam): action items: Liam send config; Priya run soak and upload traces; Ava send pricing/sec docs and SOC2 packet.
09:34 Speaker 1 (Ava): cool; any final questions?
09:38 Speaker 5 (Sophie): one tiny thing — can you include p99 for cold starts separately in the report?
09:42 Speaker 2 (Liam): yes will do.
09:45 Speaker 1 (Ava): thanks everyone, we'll follow up in thread and see results next week.

Attachments mentioned: link to config repo (repo.redwood.ai/poc/nimbus/batching-config), shared perf spreadsheet (sheets.redwood.ai/nimbus-poc), SOC2 packet link (redwood.ai/security/soc2).

End of transcript.

Post-call notes:
- Soak test scheduled: 2025-10-23 09:00 PT by Priya.
- Benchmarks to include cold-start p99, warm steady-state p95/p99, kv cache hit-rate, GPU util, and mem pressure.
- Redwood to provide updated config and cost calc.
